Jozkowski examining differences in body appreciation among women with different sexual orientations (heterosexual, bisexual, and other sexual minorities). The study found significant differences in body appreciation between sexual minority and heterosexual women when controlling for demographic characteristics, but no significant differences between bisexual women and other sexual minority women.

1._section_summary: This section describes the participants in a study with two samples collected in 2010 (Sample 1) and 2012 (Sample 2) with no overlapping data. The final analytic sample consisted of 903 women who completed the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS), after excluding those age 50+ and those with BMI >46 or <15. Sample 1 women were significantly older (M=28.9 vs 27.01), more educated (83.7% vs 55.5% with bachelor's degree or higher), and had higher BMI (M=27.78 vs 25.46) compared to Sample 2, though the samples did not differ significantly on race or sexual orientation. Overall, 86.3% of the sample identified as White and 67.1% held a bachelor's degree or higher.

6.evidence_source: The text describes analyses (bivariate analyses and ANCOVA) from a single study comparing heterosexual versus sexual minority women. No multiple studies are explicitly named or described.
6._section_summary: This section presents bivariate and ANCOVA analyses comparing heterosexual and sexual minority women on body appreciation (BAS) and related variables. Sexual minority women were significantly older (M=29.17 vs. M=27.17), had higher BMI (M=27.56 vs. M=25.61), and were more likely to have a bachelor's degree or higher. After controlling for age, BMI, sexual relationship status, and education level, sexual minority women showed significantly higher body appreciation scores (adjusted M=3.77) compared to heterosexual women (adjusted M=3.60), with BMI being the only other significant predictor of BAS.

7._section_summary: This Discussion section examines body appreciation among sexual minority women using objectification theory as a framework. The authors report that sexual minority women showed higher mean body appreciation scores than heterosexual women, though the effect size was very small (η²=.012), and that the correlation between BMI and body appreciation (BAS) was stronger for heterosexual women but not statistically significantly different (z=.41, p=.34). The study comprised two samples collected at different time points, with participants described as primarily educated White women, which the authors acknowledge as a significant limitation affecting generalizability.
